# Wiki Page Placement

A page's path and its build-order edges both follow rules the engines check. This lookup holds where each page may sit and which pages it may depend on.

**See also:** `wiki-conventions` — for how links between pages are formed and resolved.
**See also:** `wiki-structure-fields` — for the kind and depends-on fields these rules govern.

## Where a page may sit

The placement rules, each enforced by the engine it names and stated only here:

- A `test-scenario` lives at `<domain>/test-scenarios/<citation-key>.md`, where the citation key is
  the one its subject is cited by — the path is what makes a scenario page findable from the
  citation, so `/wiki-lint` checks it rather than leaving it conventional.
- No two pages claim the same citation key — a `/wiki-lint` error. A collision makes a citation
  ambiguous, and the engine cannot tell which page a `@verifies` annotation meant.
- A typed page does not sit in a root directory outside `wiki.include` — a `/wiki-lint` error. Such a
  page is invisible to every walk the engines make — index, lint, audit — so it reads as absent
  rather than as wrong.
- Every other typed page sits at one of the homes its template's `Lives at:` label declares — a
  `/wiki-conformance-audit` error, with no per-page override. A `<placeholder>` stands for a run of characters within one path
  segment, except `<module>`, which stands for one to three segments — a deliverable, then up to two
  levels of areas. A template whose label names no backticked home is a template defect the source lint
  reports, not a type left unchecked.
- Every prefix of a page's `<module>` path is a `product-module` page at `product/modules/<prefix>.md`
  — a `/wiki-conformance-audit` error naming the missing prefix. A `_shared` segment is exempt in the
  first position (wiki-level, owned by no deliverable) and the second (shared across one deliverable's
  areas), where the prefixes asked for end at the deliverable; deeper, it is checked as a real module
  name.
- A module's `kind` matches its placement — `application` or `library` at the top level of
  `product/modules/`, `area` below, and `shared` at or beneath a `_shared` segment in the first or
  second position — a `/wiki-lint` error.

## What a page may depend on

`depends-on` follows the composition direction — a `/wiki-lint`
error. Each end of an edge resolves to its deliverable, the first segment of its module path. An
edge inside one deliverable is legal, and `app-base`, which belongs to no deliverable, is a legal
target from anywhere. Across deliverables:

- a library never depends on an application, and neither does the top-level `_shared` — wiki-level
  content, owned by no deliverable, which therefore resolves as a library;
- applications depend on each other part to part: any page of one application other than its own
  page, `modules/<application>.md` — a feature, an area, or its own `_shared` content — may depend
  on a feature or area of another, and no edge between two applications starts or ends at either
  one's own page. An application's own page depends only on libraries, the top-level `_shared` and
  `app-base`;
- a deliverable's own `_shared` content, under `modules/<deliverable>/_shared/` or
  `features/<deliverable>/_shared/`, is shared across that deliverable's areas only, so no page
  outside that deliverable — the top-level `_shared` included — depends on it.

Shared content that depends on an application belongs to that application: under its own `_shared`
when only its areas use it, and as one of its features or areas when other deliverables need it.
Content other deliverables need that depends on no application sits in the top-level `_shared`.

The check judges each edge by its two ends and follows no chain of edges. Build order is acyclic
page by page, so two applications may depend on each other's features. A relationship that is not a
build-order prerequisite, such as two applications exchanging information, goes in `related:`,
which makes no ordering claim (`wiki-page-spec`).
